worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $x=f(y,z)$ with $(y,z)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂x}{∂y})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂x}{∂z})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

In this case, our surface is given by

$$
x={e}^{y}-z,\,(y,z)\in D,
$$

where 

$$
D={(y,z)\,:\,0\le y\le \frac{1}{2},\,0\le z\le {e}^{2y}},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14066535/assets/9cae5b68f77c2d79df8a81d0421146ac2bbe618c6065a457c33c86caceeb1327.png)

Now, since

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{y}-z)={e}^{y}, \\ \frac{∂x}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}({e}^{y}-z)=-1,\end{aligned}
$$

the surface area is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂x}{∂y})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂x}{∂z})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+({e}^{y})^{2}+(-1)^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{{e}^{2y}+2}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1/2}{\int }_{0}^{{e}^{2y}}\sqrt{{e}^{2y}+2}\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1/2}\sqrt{{e}^{2y}+2}\cdot z\,{|}_{z=0}^{z={e}^{2y}}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1/2}\sqrt{{e}^{2y}+2}\cdot {e}^{2y}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

Setting $u={e}^{2y}+2,$ we get $\text{d}u=2{e}^{2y}\,\text{d}y.$ Also, the limits must be changed as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & 0 & 1/2 \\ u & 3 & e+2\end{aligned}
$$

 

Substituting these into our integral, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1/2}\sqrt{{e}^{2y}+2}\cdot {e}^{2y}\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{3}^{e+2}\frac{1}{2}{u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{u}^{3/2}\,{|}_{3}^{e+2} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}((e+2)^{3/2}-{3}^{3/2}) \\  & =\frac{(e+2)^{3/2}-3\sqrt{3}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$
